title: Selection Sort
description: Selection sort is a simple sorting algorithm that repeatedly finds the minimum element from the unsorted portion and places it at the beginning. It divides the array into a sorted and an unsorted region, gradually expanding the sorted region by one element at a time.
whyItMatters: Selection sort is one of the simplest sorting algorithms to understand and implement. While not the most efficient, it teaches the concept of in-place sorting and selection. It performs well on small datasets and has the advantage of making the minimum possible number of swaps — at most n-1.

howItWorks.title: How the Algorithm Works
howItWorks.intro: Selection sort works by repeatedly finding the minimum element from the unsorted portion and swapping it with the first unsorted element.
howItWorks.step1: Scan the unsorted portion of the array to find the smallest element. Start with the first unsorted element as the current minimum.
howItWorks.step2: Compare each remaining element with the current minimum. If a smaller element is found, update the minimum index.
howItWorks.step3: After scanning the entire unsorted portion, swap the minimum element with the first unsorted element:
howItWorks.step3a: If the minimum is not already in place, swap it with the first unsorted position.
howItWorks.step3b: The sorted portion grows by one element.
howItWorks.step4: Continue finding the minimum in the remaining unsorted portion and swapping. When only one element remains unsorted, the array is fully sorted.
howItWorks.exampleStep1: Find min: 11 at index 4. Swap with 64. Array: [11, 25, 12, 22, 64].
howItWorks.exampleStep2: Find min: 12 at index 2. Swap with 25. Array: [11, 12, 25, 22, 64]. Continue: 22 swapped with 25. Result: [11, 12, 22, 25, 64].

complexityAnalysis.title: Complexity Analysis
complexityAnalysis.timeBest: O(n²) — even in the best case (already sorted), selection sort must scan the entire unsorted portion to confirm the minimum. This results in n(n-1)/2 comparisons.
complexityAnalysis.timeAverage: O(n²) — on average, each pass requires scanning the remaining unsorted elements. The number of comparisons is always n(n-1)/2 regardless of input order.
complexityAnalysis.timeWorst: O(n²) — worst case is the same as best case. Selection sort always performs the same number of comparisons, making its performance predictable.
complexityAnalysis.spaceInPlace: O(1) — selection sort works in-place, requiring only a few variables for tracking the minimum index. No additional arrays are needed.
complexityAnalysis.spaceNotStable: Not stable — equal elements may change their relative order during swapping. For example, if two equal elements are at different positions, the swap may reverse their order.
complexityAnalysis.comparison: Selection sort makes fewer swaps than bubble sort (at most n-1 vs O(n²)), but always performs O(n²) comparisons. Insertion sort is generally faster on partially sorted data. Selection sort's advantage is predictable performance — it always takes the same time regardless of input order.

applications.title: Real-World Applications
applications.app1: Selection sort is suitable for small datasets (n < 20) where its simplicity outweighs its inefficiency. It's easy to implement and debug.
applications.app2: In embedded systems or environments with limited memory, selection sort's O(1) space complexity makes it attractive when memory is more critical than speed.
applications.app3: Selection sort performs at most n-1 swaps, which is fewer than most other O(n²) sorting algorithms. This is useful when write operations are expensive (e.g., flash memory, EEPROM).
applications.app4: Selection sort is often the second sorting algorithm taught after bubble sort. It demonstrates the concept of selection and in-place sorting, helping students understand algorithmic thinking.
applications.app5: The selection approach can be adapted to find the k smallest elements without fully sorting the array. Run k passes of selection sort to get the k smallest elements in order.
